subject: Neurology
vignette: A 61-year-old right-handed man has sudden difficulty speaking after an embolic infarct. He understands questions and follows commands appropriately but speaks in short, halting phrases that omit function words. He is keenly aware of his deficit and becomes visibly frustrated.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Broca (expressive) aphasia results from a lesion of the inferior frontal gyrus (Broca area) in the dominant, usually left, hemisphere. Speech is nonfluent and telegraphic, comprehension is intact, and patients retain insight and are often frustrated by their inability to speak. This contrasts with Wernicke aphasia, in which speech is fluent but meaningless and insight is lost.

explanation_incorrect.B: Wernicke aphasia features fluent, word-salad speech with impaired comprehension and lack of insight from a superior temporal lobe lesion, the opposite of this nonfluent, insight-preserved presentation.
explanation_incorrect.C: Conduction aphasia is dominated by impaired repetition from arcuate fasciculus damage, with relatively preserved fluency and comprehension.
explanation_incorrect.D: Global aphasia combines nonfluent speech with impaired comprehension from involvement of both Broca and Wernicke areas; comprehension is intact in this patient.
explanation_incorrect.E: Dysarthria is a motor inability to articulate speech without a language deficit; this patient has a true language disturbance with preserved comprehension.

educationalObjective: Broca aphasia is nonfluent with intact comprehension and preserved insight, localizing to the dominant inferior frontal gyrus.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 55-year-old woman has a left temporal lobe infarct. She speaks in long, smoothly articulated sentences filled with incorrect words and nonsensical phrases, seemingly unaware that her speech does not make sense. She cannot follow simple verbal commands.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this patient's language disturbance?

options.text: Wernicke aphasia with impaired comprehension and absent insight
Dysarthria from a motor speech deficit

explanation_correct: Wernicke (receptive) aphasia arises from a lesion of the superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke area) in the dominant hemisphere. Speech is fluent but lacks meaning, producing a word salad; comprehension is impaired; and patients typically lack insight into their deficit. Repetition is also impaired. The smooth but nonsensical speech with absent insight is classic.

explanation_incorrect.A: Broca aphasia is nonfluent with intact comprehension and preserved insight, the opposite of this fluent, comprehension-impaired, unaware presentation.
explanation_incorrect.B: Conduction aphasia primarily impairs repetition while fluency and comprehension are relatively preserved; this patient has fluent but meaningless speech and poor comprehension.
explanation_incorrect.C: Global aphasia is nonfluent with impaired comprehension from combined Broca and Wernicke damage; this patient's speech is fluent.
explanation_incorrect.E: Dysarthria is a disorder of speech motor production, not language comprehension; this patient has a higher-order language deficit with word salad.

educationalObjective: Wernicke aphasia is fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension and no insight, localizing to the dominant superior temporal gyrus.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 49-year-old man suffers a small infarct involving the white matter tract that connects Broca and Wernicke areas. He speaks fluently and comprehends well, but he is markedly unable to repeat phrases or sentences spoken to him. Naming is relatively preserved.
question: Which aphasia syndrome does he most likely have?
explanation_correct: Conduction aphasia is caused by damage to the arcuate fasciculus, the white-matter tract connecting Broca and Wernicke areas. Its hallmark is a disproportionate impairment of repetition, with relatively preserved fluent speech and comprehension. This distinguishes it from Broca aphasia, where speech is nonfluent; Wernicke aphasia, where comprehension is impaired; and global aphasia, where both are impaired.

explanation_incorrect.A: Broca aphasia causes nonfluent, telegraphic speech with intact comprehension; repetition is not the primary deficit and fluency here is preserved.
explanation_incorrect.B: Wernicke aphasia causes fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension; comprehension is intact in this patient.
explanation_incorrect.D: Global aphasia involves both Broca and Wernicke areas with nonfluent speech and impaired comprehension; this patient's fluency and comprehension are preserved.
explanation_incorrect.E: Anomic aphasia is dominated by word-finding difficulty with preserved repetition; the defining feature here is impaired repetition from arcuate fasciculus damage.

educationalObjective: Conduction aphasia from arcuate fasciculus damage is defined by impaired repetition with preserved fluency and comprehension.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 68-year-old man sustains a large left hemisphere infarct involving both the inferior frontal and superior temporal language areas. He produces only a few stereotyped words, cannot follow commands, and cannot repeat. Separately, another patient has slurred, effortful speech but normal language comprehension and writes grammatically correct sentences.
question: Which pair of diagnoses best fits these two patients, in order?
explanation_correct: The first patient has involvement of both Broca and Wernicke areas, producing global aphasia: nonfluent speech with impaired comprehension and impaired repetition. The second patient has a motor speech deficit, dysarthria, with intact language; comprehension and written language are normal and the problem is the motor production of speech. Aphasia is a higher-order language deficit from dominant-hemisphere pathology, whereas dysarthria is a motor inability to produce speech.

explanation_incorrect.A: The first patient is not simply Broca aphasia because comprehension is impaired, and the second is not Wernicke aphasia because language abilities are intact.
explanation_incorrect.B: Conduction aphasia is defined by impaired repetition with preserved fluency and comprehension, but the first patient has neither preserved fluency nor comprehension.
explanation_incorrect.C: The first patient's speech is nonfluent rather than the fluent word salad of Wernicke aphasia, and the second is not Broca aphasia because language is intact.
explanation_incorrect.D: This reverses the assignments: the first patient has a higher-order language deficit (global aphasia) and the second has a motor speech deficit (dysarthria).

educationalObjective: Global aphasia combines nonfluent speech with impaired comprehension, while dysarthria is a motor speech deficit with intact language.
